title: Bring the research station back online
description: Restore the research station through ten short ideal DC circuit investigations. Predict, build, measure, diagnose and test more than one repair.
audience: Learners approaching A-level physics, with optional GCSE bridges; curious adult explorers welcome
level: Introduction bridging GCSE to A-level DC circuits

skills.title: Explain closed-path charge flow and distinguish current from charge
skills.criterion: Correct mechanism prediction and applicable numeric/design task with correct units; at least two fresh independent opportunities, not completion count

skills.title: Interpret potential difference as energy transferred per unit charge
skills.criterion: Fresh independently marked energy-per-charge calculation and a causal distinction from current in a new circuit; at least two opportunities, not completion count

skills.title: Predict how ideal resistance changes current
skills.criterion: Use I = V/R with correct units on a fresh configuration and state the fixed-voltage condition; at least two independent opportunities

skills.title: Explain and predict current and potential difference in series and parallel paths
skills.criterion: Independently predict fresh branch and loop readings with correct units, and justify current and energy conservation in an unfamiliar arrangement; at least two fresh opportunities

skills.title: Choose measurements that test circuit fault hypotheses
skills.criterion: On at least two fresh situations, independently select a reading that separates two circuit explanations and interpret the result with correct A or V units; exploratory meter placement alone is practice.

skills.title: Budget electrical power and energy
skills.criterion: Independently predict both power and energy for fresh ideal DC loads with W/J units and explain how current or resistance changes the budget; two distinct fresh applications, not a configured-target pass alone.

skills.title: Diagnose faults and justify repairs from circuit evidence
skills.criterion: In unfamiliar series and parallel circuits, independently choose discriminating measurements, explain a fault and verify a repair with correct units and causal reasoning; the capstone must add an open investigation.

nodes.title: Wake the beacon
nodes.prompt: The beacon is dark. Two links were opened during the storm. Make a complete conducting path to bring it online. Try either link first.
hints: Trace from one supply terminal, through the heater, and back to the other terminal.
A break anywhere in this single path stops the steady current. Find every break.
nodes.workedExample: Close both links. With the path complete, the 6 V supply drives 1 A through the 6 ohm heater. Reopening either link stops it; the heater has not used up charge.
nodes.mechanism: The supply transfers energy to charge already in the conducting circuit. A complete conducting path allows a steady current. The heater transfers energy, rather than consuming charge. In this one-path ideal circuit, the same current passes every point.
nodes.bridge: A steady current needs a complete conducting path. The source transfers energy; charge is conserved. You can return to the map and explore later.

nodes.title: What if the return link opens?
nodes.prompt: The beacon is running. Predict the steady current near the supply after only the return link opens. Then test your idea.

options.text: It keeps flowing near the supply, but not after the gap.
options.feedback: Steady charge cannot keep piling up at the gap. A break interrupts the entire single path.

options.text: It falls because the heater consumes the charge.
options.feedback: The heater transfers energy from moving charge. Charge is conserved; the missing conducting path causes the stop.

options.text: It falls to zero throughout the path.
options.feedback: Yes. A return-side break interrupts the same complete path as a supply-side break.

hints: Follow the entire path, including the return side.
nodes.workedExample: In a single loop, removing a connection on either side of the load stops the steady current everywhere.
nodes.mechanism: The supply transfers energy to charge already in the conducting circuit. A complete conducting path allows a steady current. The heater transfers energy, rather than consuming charge. In this one-path ideal circuit, the same current passes every point.
nodes.bridge: A steady current needs a complete conducting path. The source transfers energy; charge is conserved. You can return to the map and explore later.

nodes.title: Test the return-side fault
nodes.prompt: Open the return link and watch the meter. You can also compare opening the supply link, or restore the beacon again before leaving. The goal is a stopped current.
hints: Try the return link. Compare the source current with the reading across the heater.
nodes.workedExample: Open the return link. Current becomes 0 A, heater power 0 W. With just one break the source voltage appears across that break.
nodes.mechanism: The supply transfers energy to charge already in the conducting circuit. A complete conducting path allows a steady current. The heater transfers energy, rather than consuming charge. In this one-path ideal circuit, the same current passes every point.
nodes.bridge: A steady current needs a complete conducting path. The source transfers energy; charge is conserved. You can return to the map and explore later.

nodes.title: A new instrument, a new fault
nodes.prompt: A separate thermometer has one conducting loop: supply → resistor → return. Its current was 0.4 A. A wire breaks after the resistor. What is the new steady current before the resistor?

options.feedback: A single break is not a half-resistance adjustment. There is no complete conducting path.

options.text: 0 A
options.feedback: Correct. The gap breaks the complete path; its position after the resistor does not preserve current before it.
That was the current with a complete path. The break interrupts the entire steady loop.

hints: Identify whether any complete conducting path remains.
nodes.workedExample: If a single-loop wire breaks on either side of a load, the steady current is zero throughout that loop.
nodes.mechanism: The supply transfers energy to charge already in the conducting circuit. A complete conducting path allows a steady current. The heater transfers energy, rather than consuming charge. In this one-path ideal circuit, the same current passes every point.
nodes.bridge: A steady current needs a complete conducting path. The source transfers energy; charge is conserved. You can return to the map and explore later.

nodes.title: Explain the repair
nodes.prompt: A 9 V supply and a 3 ohm resistor form a closed single loop. A technician says current is smaller after the resistor because some charge is used up. Choose the causal correction.

options.text: The supply creates extra charge to replace what the resistor consumes.
options.feedback: The source transfers energy; it does not continuously create net charge to replace consumed charge.

options.text: The current decreases the farther it travels from the supply.
options.feedback: Distance from the source does not cause steady current to vanish in this ideal single loop.

options.text: Charge is conserved. The resistor transfers energy; the steady current is the same before and after it.
options.feedback: Yes. Energy is transferred to the resistor. Charge flow does not steadily disappear along a single path.

hints: Distinguish charge from the energy transferred by each unit of charge.
nodes.workedExample: One path means no branch where charge can go elsewhere. In steady state, as much charge per second leaves the resistor as enters it.
nodes.mechanism: The supply transfers energy to charge already in the conducting circuit. A complete conducting path allows a steady current. The heater transfers energy, rather than consuming charge. In this one-path ideal circuit, the same current passes every point.
nodes.bridge: A steady current needs a complete conducting path. The source transfers energy; charge is conserved. You can return to the map and explore later.

debrief.title: The beacon has a story to tell
debrief.body: You investigated why the full path matters, and what the heater transfers.

nodes.title: The recorder needs a reading
nodes.prompt: A marker counts charge passing one point in a steady loop. Make 4 C pass it. Change the observation time or the resistor. Can you find two different settings that work?
hints: Current tells you how many coulombs pass each second. Compare 1 A for 4 s with 2 A for 2 s.
At 6 V, a 6 ohm resistor gives 1 A. A 3 ohm resistor gives 2 A in this ideal model.
nodes.workedExample: At 6 V and 6 ohms, I = V/R = 1 A. In 4 s, Q = It = 4 C. At 3 ohms the current is 2 A, so 2 s also gives 4 C.
nodes.mechanism: Current is a rate of charge flow. The reading counts charge that passes a point during an interval, Q = It for a steady current. Charge is not used up by the resistor.
nodes.bridge: A closed path permits charge flow. Current says how fast charge passes a point; an observation window says for how long.

nodes.title: Longer watch, same flow
nodes.prompt: A different sensor carries a steady 1 A. The recorder watches one point for 6 s. What charge passes that point?

options.text: 1 C
options.feedback: One ampere means 1 C each second. Six seconds counts six such intervals.

options.text: 6 C
options.feedback: Yes. Q = It = 1 C/s times 6 s = 6 C.
Dividing by time would answer a different question. The total passing charge grows with the observation time.

hints: Write 1 A as 1 C per second, then count six seconds.
nodes.workedExample: If 2 A flows for 3 s, the charge passing the marker is 2 C/s times 3 s = 6 C.
nodes.mechanism: For steady flow, charge passing a point is current multiplied by elapsed time. A longer observation does not create charge; it counts more of the charge already flowing through the loop.
nodes.bridge: You can return to the circuit recorder or continue to a fresh measurement.

nodes.title: A new recorder trace
nodes.prompt: In another subsystem, 0.4 A passes a marker steadily for 15 s. How much charge passes it?

options.text: About 0.027 C
options.feedback: That divides current by time. Charge is the rate multiplied by the time.

options.text: 6 C
options.feedback: Correct. 0.4 C/s times 15 s is 6 C.
That divides the 15 s by 0.4 A. The unit C/s times s gives C.

hints: An ampere is a coulomb per second. Multiply by the observation time.
nodes.workedExample: For 0.5 A over 8 s, Q = It = 0.5 C/s times 8 s = 4 C.
nodes.mechanism: The same rate-times-time relationship applies to an unfamiliar subsystem. A correct first attempt without revealed help is one piece of evidence, not a whole-skill certificate.
nodes.bridge: The total charge counted depends on both rate and duration. Next, reason about where that charge goes.

nodes.title: Where did the charge go?
nodes.prompt: A closed single-loop heater carries a steady 0.8 A into the resistor. What rate of charge leaves it at the other end?

options.text: Less than 0.8 A, because some charge becomes heat
options.feedback: The resistor transfers electrical energy to thermal energy. It does not consume charge in steady state.

options.text: 0.8 A, because charge is conserved in the single steady path
options.feedback: Yes. Equal charge per second enters and leaves the resistor in this steady single loop.

options.text: More than 0.8 A, because the source replaces charge
options.feedback: The source transfers energy to charge; it does not make extra steady current after the resistor.

hints: Separate the movement of charge from energy transferred to the heater.
nodes.workedExample: If 2 C enters a resistor in 2 s in a steady single loop, 2 C also leaves it in those 2 s. The current is 1 A on each side.
nodes.mechanism: A steady single path cannot accumulate charge indefinitely at the resistor. Current is equal around that path, while energy is transferred in the resistor.
nodes.bridge: The recorder gave you a rate and a total. The next investigation asks what energy each coulomb receives.

debrief.title: A useful rate
debrief.body: You used a charge counter to connect amperes, coulombs and seconds, then checked that the resistor transfers energy rather than consuming charge.

nodes.title: Set the energy lift
nodes.prompt: The console watches a 6 ohm ideal load for 4 s. Set the supply so each coulomb receives 6 J and the source transfers 24 J in the window. Explore what changes when the voltage changes.
hints: A potential difference of 1 V means 1 J transferred per coulomb. First find the setting that gives 6 J/C.
At 6 V across 6 ohms, the current is 1 A. In 4 s, 4 C passes the load.
nodes.workedExample: At 6 V across 6 ohms, I = 1 A. In 4 s, Q = 4 C. Energy transferred is VQ = 6 J/C times 4 C = 24 J.
nodes.mechanism: Potential difference describes energy transferred per coulomb. Here the fixed ideal resistance also makes current change when voltage changes. Total energy over an interval depends on both the energy per charge and how much charge passes.
nodes.bridge: The recorder counted coulombs. Voltage now tells you the energy transferred for each coulomb.

nodes.title: Read a different lift
nodes.prompt: A source transfers 12 J to 2 C of charge. What potential difference did that charge cross?

options.text: 6 V
options.feedback: Yes. 12 J divided by 2 C is 6 J/C, or 6 V.
That multiplies energy by charge. Potential difference is energy per unit charge.

options.text: About 0.17 V
options.feedback: That reverses the ratio. Divide energy by charge, not charge by energy.

hints: What does per coulomb mean in a numerical ratio?
nodes.workedExample: If 9 J is transferred to 3 C, the potential difference is 9 J / 3 C = 3 V.
nodes.mechanism: Potential difference is energy transferred per unit charge, V = E/Q. It does not by itself tell you how much charge flows each second.
nodes.bridge: Now use the same principle with a new source rather than the console settings.

nodes.title: The backup source
nodes.prompt: The backup source transfers 15 J while 3 C passes through it. What is its potential difference?

options.feedback: That multiplies joules and coulombs. Volts are joules per coulomb.

options.text: 5 V
options.feedback: Correct. 15 J / 3 C = 5 J/C = 5 V.
That divides 3 C by 15 J. The source's energy per coulomb is 15 divided by 3.

hints: Divide the transferred energy by the passing charge.
nodes.workedExample: If 20 J goes to 4 C, V = 20 J / 4 C = 5 V.
nodes.mechanism: The 5 V describes 5 J transferred for each coulomb. A different current could flow depending on the connected circuit.
nodes.bridge: Energy per charge and charge per second have different units and answer different questions.

nodes.title: Same rate, different lift?
nodes.prompt: Circuit A uses 6 V across 6 ohms. Circuit B uses 12 V across 12 ohms. Both are ideal single loops. Which statement is true?

options.text: Both have 1 A, so each coulomb receives the same energy
options.feedback: Both currents are 1 A, but the source potential differences are 6 J/C and 12 J/C.

options.text: The 12 V circuit must have twice the current
options.feedback: Its resistance also doubles. In each ideal loop, I = V/R = 1 A.

options.text: Both have 1 A, but each coulomb receives more energy in circuit B
options.feedback: Yes. The same charge per second passes, while circuit B supplies 12 J per coulomb rather than 6 J.

hints: Calculate V/R for each circuit, then compare the volts as joules per coulomb.
nodes.workedExample: A 4 V source across 4 ohms and an 8 V source across 8 ohms both give 1 A, but the energy supplied per coulomb is 4 J and 8 J respectively.
nodes.mechanism: Current and potential difference are distinct. The resistance determines how a particular ideal circuit responds to the source's energy per charge.
nodes.bridge: The next investigation lets you tune both supply and resistance to control current.

debrief.title: Energy for every coulomb
debrief.body: You linked volts to joules per coulomb and separated that idea from amperes, the rate of charge flow.

nodes.title: Keep the heater in range
nodes.prompt: The ideal sensor heater needs a steady 1 A. Tune supply voltage and resistance. There are two settings that work. Find both, then decide why they agree.
hints: For this ideal resistor, current is supply voltage divided by resistance.
A 6 V supply with 6 ohms gives the same current as 12 V with 12 ohms.
nodes.workedExample: At 6 V and 6 ohms, I = V/R = 1 A. At 12 V and 12 ohms, I = 1 A again. The ratio stays equal even though voltage and resistance both change.
nodes.mechanism: In an ideal ohmic loop, I = V/R. At fixed voltage, more resistance means less current. If the supply voltage changes too, compare the whole ratio rather than one setting alone.
nodes.bridge: The source sets energy per charge; the load's ideal resistance determines the steady current for that voltage.

nodes.title: Two ways to one ampere
nodes.prompt: Why do both 6 V across 6 ohms and 12 V across 12 ohms produce 1 A in this ideal model?

options.text: An ideal source always supplies 1 A
options.feedback: The source fixes voltage here. Its current depends on the connected resistance.

options.text: Voltage and resistance rise together, leaving V/R at 1 A
options.feedback: Yes. 6/6 and 12/12 both equal 1 A.

options.text: Resistance does not affect current
options.feedback: Hold voltage at 6 V and change 6 ohms to 12 ohms: current falls from 1 A to 0.5 A.

hints: Calculate V/R for each setting rather than comparing voltage alone.
nodes.workedExample: At 8 V with 4 ohms, I = 2 A. At 16 V with 8 ohms, I = 2 A again.
nodes.mechanism: The same current can result from different pairs of voltage and resistance. This does not mean the source forces a constant current in every circuit.
nodes.bridge: Use a new supply setting to predict a change before viewing a readout.

nodes.title: A different heater
nodes.prompt: A 9 V ideal source drives a 3 ohm resistor. The resistor is replaced with 6 ohms while the source stays at 9 V. What is the new current?

options.feedback: Correct. 9 V / 6 ohms = 1.5 A, half the original 3 A.

options.text: 3 A
options.feedback: That was the current with 3 ohms. At fixed voltage, doubling resistance halves current.

options.text: 6 A
options.feedback: More resistance at the same voltage cannot double the current in this ideal ohmic circuit.

hints: Keep 9 V fixed and divide by the new 6 ohms.
nodes.workedExample: At 12 V, changing 4 ohms to 8 ohms changes current from 3 A to 1.5 A.
nodes.mechanism: The comparison holds voltage fixed. I = V/R gives 1.5 A after the resistance doubles.
nodes.bridge: The rule about resistance needs its fixed-voltage condition.

nodes.title: A rule with a condition
nodes.prompt: A colleague says: doubling resistance always halves current. Which correction fits ideal ohmic circuits?

options.text: The claim is true even if the supply voltage changes
options.feedback: If voltage doubles too, V/R and current can stay the same.

options.text: It is true when the potential difference is held fixed
options.feedback: Yes. I = V/R; at fixed V, doubling R halves I.

options.text: Resistance never affects current
options.feedback: At a fixed source voltage, changing resistance changes current in this ideal model.

hints: Ask which quantity besides resistance appears in I = V/R.
nodes.workedExample: 6 V / 3 ohms = 2 A; 6 V / 6 ohms = 1 A. But 12 V / 6 ohms = 2 A again.
nodes.mechanism: Physics comparisons must state what stays fixed. The ideal resistor relation is useful within its model boundary, not a universal claim for every component.
nodes.bridge: Next, follow current and energy around a path with more than one load.

debrief.title: A ratio worth testing
debrief.body: You used voltage and resistance together to set current and qualified the fixed-voltage rule. The load is an ideal resistor, not a realistic lamp.

nodes.title: Tune two loads in one path
nodes.prompt: The station signal must run at 1 A through two ideal coils on one path. Set their resistances. Either coil can be the larger one. Compare the current and each voltage drop in the meter table before moving on.
hints: One path means both resistances contribute to the same total.
At 12 V, a total of 12 ohms gives 1 A. You can put 9 ohms in either coil.
nodes.workedExample: With 3 ohms and 9 ohms in series, total resistance is 12 ohms, so source current is 12 V / 12 ohms = 1 A. The same 1 A flows through both coils. Their voltage drops are 3 V and 9 V.
nodes.mechanism: In a steady one-path ideal circuit, charge has no junction at which to split, so current is the same in each load. Each load transfers a share of the source energy per charge; those voltage drops add to 12 V.
nodes.bridge: One path shares current. Voltage drops depend on each resistance and add back to the supply voltage.

nodes.title: Where does the energy go?
nodes.prompt: You found 1 A through a 3 ohm coil followed by a 9 ohm coil on a 12 V supply. Which pair of voltage drops should the meters show?

options.text: 3 V then 9 V; together they account for 12 V
options.feedback: Yes. With 1 A through each load, V = IR gives 3 V and 9 V. Their sum matches the source.

options.text: 6 V then 6 V because the source divides equally between two loads
options.feedback: Equal drops need equal resistances at the same current. These loads are 3 and 9 ohms.

options.text: 12 V across each coil because each receives the full supply
options.feedback: That describes parallel branches. These coils share one path, so their drops sum to 12 V.

hints: Use V = IR for each coil, then add the drops.
nodes.workedExample: At 1 A, a 2 ohm coil drops 2 V and a 10 ohm coil drops 10 V. The total is the 12 V supply.
nodes.mechanism: The source gives 12 J to each coulomb. The two loads together transfer that 12 J per coulomb, split in proportion to their resistances at the common current.
nodes.bridge: Series loads share current, but each load may transfer a different amount of energy per coulomb.

nodes.title: Turn the path around
nodes.prompt: The station asks whether position changes the current. Move the 9 ohm setting to the front and the 3 ohm setting to the rear. Compare the two meter rows; the first coil should now drop 9 V while source current stays 1 A.
hints: Change both coils so the total stays at 12 ohms.
With the front coil at 9 ohms and 1 A, it drops 9 V. The rear must be 3 ohms to keep 1 A.
nodes.workedExample: At 9 ohms plus 3 ohms, the total is still 12 ohms and the source still drives 1 A. The front now drops 9 V and the rear 3 V.
nodes.mechanism: Reordering ideal series loads changes where the voltage drops occur, not the total resistance or shared current. Real wires and non-ohmic devices can complicate this simple model.
nodes.bridge: Check a new path without relying on the old numbers.

nodes.title: A different station rail
nodes.prompt: A 15 V supply drives a 5 ohm load and a 10 ohm load in series. What current passes through the second load, and what potential difference is across it?

options.text: 1 A and 10 V
options.feedback: Correct. The total is 15 ohms, so both loads carry 1 A; the 10 ohm load drops 10 V.

options.text: 1 A and 5 V
options.feedback: The common current is 1 A, but 5 V is the drop across the 5 ohm load, not the 10 ohm load.

options.text: 1.5 A and 15 V
options.feedback: The 10 ohm load does not receive the full 15 V by itself. First add the series resistances: 5 + 10 = 15 ohms.

hints: Add the series resistances before dividing supply voltage by the total.
nodes.workedExample: For 18 V across 6 ohms and 3 ohms in series, total resistance is 9 ohms, current is 2 A and the 3 ohm load drops 6 V.
nodes.mechanism: One-path current is common to both loads. The drops are 5 V and 10 V, which account for the 15 V source.
nodes.bridge: Test whether the one-path rule survives a break.

nodes.title: One gap, two quiet loads
nodes.prompt: A connector between two ideal series loads opens. What happens to the steady current through the load before the gap and the load after it?

options.text: Both currents fall to zero
options.feedback: Yes. An open connection breaks the only complete path, so steady current stops everywhere in that path.

options.text: The first load still carries current, but the second does not
options.feedback: Charge cannot keep accumulating at the gap in this steady model. The whole single path is interrupted.

options.text: The second load still carries current from stored charge
options.feedback: Neither ideal resistor supplies charge or a closed return path. This model has no storage element.

hints: Trace a complete route from the source and back.
nodes.workedExample: If a switch opens anywhere in a single series loop, no complete conducting path remains, so current through every load is zero.
nodes.mechanism: A break in the only route stops the steady loop; contrast this with a later parallel circuit, where another complete branch may remain.
nodes.bridge: Next, let the station make two complete routes and see what a branch break changes.

debrief.title: One path, shared current
debrief.body: You changed resistance and watched one current pass through both ideal loads. Their potential differences divided the source energy per charge and added to the supply voltage.

nodes.title: Bring the backup branch online
nodes.prompt: The main rail runs through a 6 ohm ideal load at 6 V. The backup branch is open. Close its link and watch the source current and both branch currents. Then try reopening it; does the main branch go quiet?
hints: The open backup branch has no steady current, but the main branch still has a full route.
When both 6 ohm branches have 6 V across them, each carries 1 A; add them at the junction.
nodes.workedExample: Main alone: 6 V / 6 ohms = 1 A. Closing the backup makes a second 6 V / 6 ohm route carrying 1 A. The source supplies 2 A in total.
nodes.mechanism: Parallel branches share the same two junctions, so each ideal branch sees the full supply voltage. Charge flow into the split equals the sum of branch currents; an open backup does not break the intact main route.
nodes.bridge: Keep the backup open while you predict the main rail.

nodes.title: Does the main rail notice?
nodes.prompt: With two 6 ohm branches at 6 V, each carries 1 A. The backup link opens. What are the new main-branch and source currents in this ideal fixed-voltage circuit?

options.text: Main 1 A; source 1 A
options.feedback: Exactly. The main branch still has 6 V across 6 ohms. Only the backup current disappears.

options.text: Main 0 A; source 0 A
options.feedback: The backup has opened, but the main branch remains a complete route across the source.

options.text: Main 2 A; source 2 A
options.feedback: The main branch still has 6 V across 6 ohms, so it remains at 1 A. Source current is now just that one branch.

hints: The ideal source holds 6 V across the still-complete main branch.
nodes.workedExample: At 10 V, a 5 ohm main branch stays at 2 A when a separate backup branch opens; source current loses only the backup contribution.
nodes.mechanism: For a fixed ideal source, removing one parallel route reduces source current, but need not change the voltage or current in another intact branch.
nodes.bridge: Now control which route consumes the current budget.

nodes.title: Spend only three amperes
nodes.prompt: Both station branches are complete at 12 V. At 6 ohms each, source current is 4 A. Adjust either branch so the total becomes 3 A, and compare the two ways to distribute it.
hints: At fixed 12 V, a 6 ohm branch takes 2 A and a 12 ohm branch takes 1 A.
Keep one branch at 6 ohms and set the other to 12 ohms. Swapping which branch is limited also works.
nodes.workedExample: At 12 V, the 6 ohm branch carries 2 A and the 12 ohm branch carries 1 A. The junction adds them to 3 A. Either branch can be the 12 ohm one.
nodes.mechanism: Changing one parallel branch changes that branch current and the source total. The other branch still sees the fixed 12 V in this ideal source model.
nodes.bridge: Make a fresh branch calculation without the visible readout.

nodes.title: A new junction
nodes.prompt: A 9 V ideal source feeds 3 ohms in one branch and 6 ohms in another. Both branches are complete. What current leaves the source?

options.feedback: Correct. The branch currents are 9/3 = 3 A and 9/6 = 1.5 A; together they are 4.5 A.

options.text: 3 A
options.feedback: That is only the current through the 3 ohm branch. The source also feeds the 6 ohm branch.
That is only the current through the 6 ohm branch. Add the 3 A in the other branch.

hints: Each branch has 9 V across it. Find both currents, then add them.
nodes.workedExample: For two complete branches at 12 V with 4 ohms and 6 ohms, currents are 3 A and 2 A, so source current is 5 A.
nodes.mechanism: The 9 V source maintains the same potential difference across both ideal branches. Their separate charge-flow rates add at the source junction.
nodes.bridge: One last fault, this time with a surviving path.

nodes.title: A backup fuse opens
nodes.prompt: A 10 V ideal source feeds two complete branches: 5 ohms in the main branch and 10 ohms in the backup. The backup fuse opens. What happens to the main current and source total?

options.text: Main stays 2 A; source falls from 3 A to 2 A
options.feedback: Yes. Main remains at 10/5 = 2 A. The 1 A backup contribution disappears from the source total.

options.text: Main falls to 0 A; source falls to 0 A
options.feedback: The main branch is still a complete route across 10 V. Opening another branch does not break it.

options.text: Main rises to 3 A; source stays at 3 A
options.feedback: The ideal source holds the main branch at 10 V, so its 5 ohms still carry 2 A. The backup current no longer contributes.

hints: Check which route actually contains the open fuse.
nodes.workedExample: At 6 V, a 3 ohm main route carries 2 A even after a separate 6 ohm backup route opens; the source total falls from 3 A to 2 A.
nodes.mechanism: Conservation holds at the split: source current is the sum of complete-branch currents. A break removes its branch contribution without consuming charge in the other route.
nodes.bridge: The next investigation will ask which meter reading can distinguish a fault from a normal load change.

debrief.title: More than one way home
debrief.body: You kept an intact branch running while another opened, and balanced source current as the sum of separate branch currents. The ideal source held each branch at the same voltage.

nodes.title: The silent backup
nodes.prompt: The station backup is quiet, but the main rail is still live. Is the backup branch intact, or has its link opened? Choose a meter position that could tell. Try a tempting but unhelpful reading too: why does it fail?

candidates.title: Backup branch has an open link

hints: The main branch is across the same ideal 12 V supply in either case. Would its current change?
A branch current or potential difference across the uncertain link responds directly to an open backup route.
nodes.workedExample: With 12 V across a 12 ohm main route, its current is 1 A either way. A complete 12 ohm backup adds 1 A, giving 2 A at the source; an open backup adds 0 A, leaving 1 A. A meter in the backup or at the source can distinguish them.
nodes.mechanism: An ideal ammeter reads charge flow per second at its position; an ideal voltmeter reads potential difference across two points. A useful observation is one for which the competing explanations predict different values.
nodes.bridge: If the branch picture is confusing, reopen the previous parallel-routes episode. You can still continue with help without an independent pass.

nodes.title: Read the clue
nodes.prompt: Open Earlier field readings below if you want to revisit your measurements. Which explanation fits the observed circuit?

options.text: The backup link is open; the main route still carries 1 A.
options.feedback: Yes. The intact main branch stays at 1 A, while the backup adds no current.

options.text: Both branches are open, so every current is 0 A.
options.feedback: The main route is complete. Its 12 V across 12 ohms still gives 1 A.

options.text: Both branches are intact, so the source carries 2 A.
options.feedback: That would be the intact-backup prediction. Compare it with the meter reading you chose.

hints: Compare the actual reading with each candidate prediction shown after your probe.
nodes.workedExample: If the backup link opens, the main 12 ohm branch remains across 12 V and carries 1 A. Backup current is 0 A, so source current is 1 A.
nodes.mechanism: Use the reading as evidence, not merely the fact that the backup looks dark. The branch structure explains why the main rail survives.
nodes.bridge: Now make a measurement decision in a different subsystem before its reading is revealed.

nodes.title: A sensor with two stories
nodes.prompt: A new 12 V panel has a 6 ohm navigation rail in parallel with a sensor heater. The heater could be 12 ohms or 24 ohms. Which single position tests that change directly? Decide before taking a new reading.

options.text: An ammeter in series with the sensor heater
options.feedback: Correct. The heater current would be 1 A at 12 ohms or 0.5 A at 24 ohms.

options.text: An ammeter in the unchanged navigation rail
options.feedback: That rail stays at 12/6 = 2 A under either heater hypothesis.

options.text: A voltmeter across the ideal 12 V supply
options.feedback: The ideal supply remains at 12 V for both heater values.

options.text: A voltmeter across the unchanged navigation rail
options.feedback: Both branches remain across 12 V, so this cannot separate the heater values.

hints: At fixed 12 V, ask which quantity responds when only the sensor resistance changes.
nodes.workedExample: For a separate 10 V branch, a change from 5 to 10 ohms would shift branch current from 2 to 1 A. The unchanged branch and ideal supply voltage would not reveal which value it has.
nodes.mechanism: The current through the changing branch follows I = V/R. An informative measurement has different predicted results for the two hypotheses.
nodes.bridge: The parallel-routes episode shows why the unchanged rail current is a poor test.

nodes.title: Check your prediction
nodes.prompt: Now choose a meter in the new panel. You may compare the sensor ammeter with a position that hides the change. Which heater value is supported by the observed reading?

candidates.title: Sensor heater has drifted to 24 ohms

hints: Both sensor possibilities have 12 V across the heater. Divide by 12 or 24 ohms to predict its current.
An ideal 12 V source supplies 2 A to the 6 ohm rail in both cases; sensor current changes from 1 to 0.5 A.
nodes.workedExample: The navigation rail takes 12/6 = 2 A. The sensor takes 1 A at 12 ohms or 0.5 A at 24 ohms. The observed 0.5 A sensor current supports the 24 ohm state.
nodes.mechanism: A voltage reading across either complete parallel branch remains 12 V; current in the changing branch is diagnostic. The supply current also changes, but includes both branches.
nodes.bridge: One final unfamiliar circuit tests whether you can interpret a meter result without the candidate table.

nodes.title: The resistor that changed
nodes.prompt: A different 9 V unit has two resistors in series: the known one is 3 ohms, and the hidden one is either 3 or 6 ohms. An ideal ammeter at the supply reads 1 A. Which hidden value is supported?

options.text: 6 ohms; total resistance is 9 ohms.
options.feedback: Yes. In one series path, 9 V / 1 A = 9 ohms total. Subtract 3 ohms to find the hidden 6 ohms.

options.text: 3 ohms; total resistance is 6 ohms.
options.feedback: That would predict 9/6 = 1.5 A, not the observed 1 A.

options.text: 9 ohms; the ammeter reads the hidden resistor alone.
options.feedback: The 9 ohms is the total series resistance. The known 3 ohms is part of it.

hints: Use R_total = V/I from the actual meter reading, then subtract the known series resistance.
nodes.workedExample: For an 8 V series circuit reading 1 A, total resistance is 8 ohms. If a known resistor is 2 ohms, the hidden resistor is 6 ohms.
nodes.mechanism: The ammeter sees the same current throughout a single series path. Its reading constrains the total resistance, which can be compared with the competing hidden values.
nodes.bridge: Return to the series-path episode for a worked current and voltage split.

nodes.title: Write the lab rule
nodes.prompt: Before leaving, choose the rule you would take into an unfamiliar investigation.

options.text: Predict each candidate reading first; measure where their predictions differ, then check units and circuit topology.
options.feedback: Exactly. The meter is useful because it can separate explanations, not because it produces a number.

options.text: Always measure where the number is largest.
options.feedback: A large reading can be identical under both explanations and tell you nothing about the fault.

options.text: Measure only the source voltage in an ideal fixed-voltage circuit.
options.feedback: The same source voltage may occur under both hypotheses. The reading must be able to discriminate.

hints: A useful observation could rule out at least one possible explanation.
nodes.workedExample: If two possible branch faults both leave a main current at 1 A, measuring there cannot distinguish them. Choose a position whose predicted readings differ.
nodes.mechanism: Your next station task can combine meter evidence with a repair. Real meters load circuits slightly; this pilot uses ideal instruments and steady ohmic components.
nodes.bridge: You can revisit either meter panel to try a different order of measurements.

debrief.title: A meter is a question
debrief.body: You tested where rival circuit explanations predict different readings, interpreted two unfamiliar results, and learned why some perfectly valid readings are useless for a particular diagnosis. The station model uses ideal meters and fixed-voltage, steady DC circuits.

nodes.title: Two ways to warm a sensor
nodes.prompt: The shelter heater needs 12 W. Change its ideal supply or resistance until it reaches that power. Then find another setting that also gives 12 W: do the two settings draw the same current?
hints: Power is energy transferred each second. Look at source voltage and current together: P = VI.
At 6 V, 3 ohms takes 2 A; at 12 V, 12 ohms takes 1 A. Both transfer 12 J each second.
nodes.workedExample: At 6 V and 3 ohms, I = 2 A and P = 12 W. At 12 V and 12 ohms, I = 1 A and P = 12 W. The starting 6 V and 12 ohms makes only 3 W.
nodes.mechanism: Equal power does not mean equal current or equal potential difference. The product VI is the rate of energy transfer for each load.
nodes.bridge: If you need the current/resistance bridge, revisit Tune the sensor heater.

nodes.title: Same watts, different flow
nodes.prompt: You found 12 W at either 6 V with 3 ohms or 12 V with 12 ohms. Which comparison is correct?

options.text: Both are 12 W, but the 6 V setting draws 2 A while the 12 V setting draws 1 A.
options.feedback: Yes. 6×2 and 12×1 both make 12 W.

options.text: Both are 12 W and both draw 2 A.
options.feedback: At 12 V across 12 ohms, current is 1 A, not 2 A.

options.text: The 12 V setting must use twice the power because voltage doubled.
options.feedback: Resistance also changed. Compute both currents and multiply V by I.

hints: Compute I = V/R for each configuration, then P = VI.
nodes.workedExample: A 4 V load at 2 A and an 8 V load at 1 A both use 8 W, despite different currents.
nodes.mechanism: A watt is a joule per second; different voltage/current pairs can transfer energy at the same rate.
nodes.bridge: Now share a fixed source budget between two live systems.

nodes.title: Keep the station under budget
nodes.prompt: At 6 V the navigation rail is too weak. Give its fixed 12 ohm load 12 W, keep the sensor heater at 6 W, and observe exactly 180 J transferred by the source in your chosen observation window. Explore which control changes each quantity.
hints: At 12 V, the 12 ohm navigation rail takes 1 A and 12 W.
Give the sensor 24 ohms: at 12 V it takes 0.5 A and 6 W. Total 18 W for 10 s is 180 J.
nodes.workedExample: At 12 V, navigation P = V²/R = 144/12 = 12 W; sensor with 24 ohms uses 144/24 = 6 W. Total 18 W over 10 s is 180 J.
nodes.mechanism: Both complete parallel loads receive the same ideal 12 V. The source supplies the sum of their power, and energy depends on how long that rate continues. The model does not simulate battery depletion.
nodes.bridge: If you need to see each load separately, open the path and meter table.

nodes.title: A fresh four-second pulse
nodes.prompt: A different 12 V panel draws 1.5 A for 4 s at steady current. How much electrical energy does its source transfer?

options.feedback: Correct. P = 12 V × 1.5 A = 18 W, then E = 18 W × 4 s = 72 J.
18 W is the rate each second. Multiply by the 4 s observation window.

options.text: 6 J
options.feedback: 1.5 A × 4 s gives 6 C of charge, not energy. Each coulomb carries 12 J here.
That omits the 1.5 A factor. Multiply potential difference, current and time.

hints: First find the rate in watts using P = VI; then multiply by seconds.
nodes.workedExample: At 10 V and 2 A, power is 20 W. Over 3 s, energy is 60 J.
nodes.mechanism: For a steady ideal circuit, P = VI and E = Pt; a watt is one joule per second. Charge is a different quantity with C units.
nodes.bridge: One more unfamiliar case tests the mechanism behind a power change.

nodes.title: The resistor doubles
nodes.prompt: An ideal 12 V supply stays fixed. A single ohmic load changes from 6 ohms to 12 ohms while the observation time stays the same. What happens to its power and energy over that time?

options.text: Both power and energy halve.
options.feedback: Yes. Current falls from 2 A to 1 A, so power falls from 24 W to 12 W; over the same time, energy halves.

options.text: They stay the same because voltage stays at 12 V.
options.feedback: At fixed voltage, doubling resistance halves current. P = VI then changes.

options.text: Both double because resistance doubled.
options.feedback: At fixed voltage, a larger ideal resistance reduces current, so power falls.

options.text: They fall to zero because higher resistance is an open gap.
options.feedback: 12 ohms is finite, so steady current still flows.

hints: Calculate current before and after from I = V/R.
nodes.workedExample: At 8 V, changing an ideal resistor from 4 to 8 ohms reduces current from 2 to 1 A and power from 16 to 8 W.
nodes.mechanism: Under a fixed ideal supply and ohmic conditions, P = V²/R; doubling resistance halves the rate. Equal observation times preserve that factor for energy.
nodes.bridge: Return to the resistance bridge if the fixed-voltage assumption is unclear.

nodes.title: Name the two budgets
nodes.prompt: Before the repair desk, choose the distinction the technician must keep straight.

options.text: Power is the transfer rate in W; energy is that rate accumulated over time in J.
options.feedback: Exactly. A 12 W load uses 12 J each second while the ideal steady conditions last.

options.text: Power and energy are the same number in different units.
options.feedback: Only for a one-second window do their numerical values happen to coincide.

options.text: Power is charge flow in C; energy is current in A.
options.feedback: C and A describe charge and charge rate, not power or energy.

hints: Ask whether the quantity is per second or accumulated.
nodes.workedExample: A 5 W load running for 3 s transfers 15 J.
nodes.mechanism: The station may budget an instantaneous power rate and a finite observation-window energy separately.
nodes.bridge: The next episode uses measurements to decide why a system misses its power target.

debrief.title: The watts have a cost
debrief.body: You found equal power with different current and potential difference, shared a two-branch power budget and made fresh energy and fixed-voltage predictions. These ideal steady loads do not model battery depletion or heating-dependent resistance.

nodes.title: Two faults, one dim backup
nodes.prompt: The main rail is live but source current has fallen. Is the backup link open, or is its heater still connected at a higher resistance? Choose a meter that separates the stories; also try one that does not.

candidates.title: Backup link is open; its heater is 12 ohms
Backup link is closed; its heater has drifted to 24 ohms

hints: The fixed 12 V source gives the main 12 ohm rail 1 A in either case.
An open backup carries 0 A. A closed 24 ohm backup across 12 V carries 0.5 A.
nodes.workedExample: Open link: main 1 A, backup 0 A, source 1 A. Closed link with 24 ohm heater: main 1 A, backup 0.5 A, source 1.5 A. The main current and ideal supply voltage cannot distinguish them.
nodes.mechanism: A single dim symptom can have several causes. The useful meter position is the one where candidate predictions differ. An ideal source can hold the main rail live while another branch changes.
nodes.bridge: The previous measurement episode shows why identical predicted readings are unhelpful.

nodes.title: Name the supported fault
nodes.prompt: Open Earlier field readings if needed. Which explanation best matches the measured circuit?

options.text: The backup link is closed, but the heater is 24 ohms.
options.feedback: Yes. The backup still carries 0.5 A; an open link would give 0 A.

options.text: The backup link is open and its heater still has 12 ohms.
options.feedback: An open backup cannot carry the measured nonzero current in this ideal model.

options.text: The main rail is open, so the source has only backup current.
options.feedback: The complete main 12 ohm route still takes 1 A at 12 V.

hints: Compare the observed backup or source current with both predictions.
nodes.workedExample: At 12 V a complete 24 ohm backup takes 0.5 A. An open backup takes 0 A. A 12 ohm main remains at 1 A.
nodes.mechanism: A lower source current does not by itself say where the fault is; the branch reading and topology support the diagnosis.
nodes.bridge: If the observation is unclear, return to the meter panel and try a branch-specific probe.

nodes.title: Repair and deliberately break it again
nodes.prompt: The backup heater is still connected but drifted to 24 ohms. Restore the station to 2 A from the 12 V source. You may also open the backup link first to see how a second fault would change the reading, then reverse it.
hints: The main route stays at 1 A. The backup must add another 1 A to reach 2 A.
At 12 V, a complete 12 ohm backup takes 1 A and 12 W. Keep the link closed.
nodes.workedExample: Closed 24 ohm backup: 0.5 A and 6 W. Open link: 0 A backup. Closed 12 ohm backup: 1 A and 12 W, added to 1 A main gives 2 A source.
nodes.mechanism: A repair should predict and restore a measurement, not merely change a labelled part. In this ideal branch, reducing resistance increases backup current and power; opening its link cuts only that branch.
nodes.bridge: Now choose a test in a different circuit before seeing its result.

nodes.title: A fault in one series path
nodes.prompt: A fresh 12 V panel has a separate 6 ohm reference branch. Its suspect branch has a known 6 ohm resistor in series with a hidden load that is either 6 or 12 ohms. Which single measurement distinguishes the two hidden states?

options.text: An ammeter in the suspect series branch
options.feedback: Yes. Its total resistance is 12 or 18 ohms, so its current is 1 A or about 0.667 A.

options.text: An ammeter in the separate 6 ohm reference branch
options.feedback: That branch still has 12 V across 6 ohms and carries 2 A in either hidden state.

options.text: A voltmeter across the ideal 12 V supply
options.feedback: The source stays at 12 V in both states.

options.text: A voltmeter across the reference branch
options.feedback: Both possibilities leave 12 V across the complete reference branch.

hints: The reference branch stays fixed across the ideal 12 V supply. Which branch changes its total resistance?
nodes.workedExample: At 9 V, a separate 3 ohm reference branch stays at 3 A, while a suspect branch of 3 ohms plus a hidden 3 or 6 ohms carries 1.5 or 1 A. Measure the suspect branch.
nodes.mechanism: The suspect series path has one shared current that changes with its total resistance. The separate reference path remains at fixed voltage and resistance, so its readings cannot distinguish the hidden load.
nodes.bridge: The final check asks you to read evidence from a new parallel fault.

nodes.title: A fresh backup clue
nodes.prompt: A 10 V ideal source feeds a 5 ohm main branch and a backup that is either an open link or a complete 10 ohm resistor. A source ammeter reads 2 A. What is the supported diagnosis, and why?

options.text: The backup link is open; the 5 ohm main alone takes 2 A.
options.feedback: Correct. Main current is 10/5 = 2 A; a complete 10 ohm backup would add 1 A, making 3 A at the source.

options.text: The backup is complete; its 10 ohms adds no current.
options.feedback: At 10 V a complete 10 ohm branch adds 1 A, so source current would be 3 A.

options.text: Both branches are open; source current must be 0 A.
options.feedback: The observed 2 A is exactly what the complete 5 ohm main branch takes.

options.text: The source has become 2 V; its current is fixed at 2 A.
options.feedback: The problem specifies a 10 V ideal supply. Current follows the connected resistance.

hints: Compute the main branch current first; then ask whether the backup contributes.
nodes.workedExample: At 6 V, a 3 ohm main alone draws 2 A; adding a complete 6 ohm backup would make 3 A source current.
nodes.mechanism: The observed source current equals the surviving main route, so the backup adds none. Under the stated ideal fixed-voltage assumptions, an open backup explains it.
nodes.bridge: Review the parallel-routes branch-survival scene if this junction sum is uncertain.

nodes.title: What makes a repair credible?
nodes.prompt: Choose the field rule you would bring to the final station repair.

options.text: Compare fault predictions, measure where they differ, repair, then check the predicted circuit reading.
options.feedback: Yes. That sequence links a change in the circuit to evidence rather than to a guess.

options.text: Swap every part until a light turns on.
options.feedback: That may hide a second fault and gives weak evidence about the mechanism.

options.text: Always read only the ideal source voltage.
options.feedback: Several different faults can leave that supply reading unchanged.

hints: A useful repair has a falsifiable before-and-after prediction.
nodes.workedExample: If a closed 12 ohm branch at 12 V should add 1 A, a repair that restores it should raise source current by 1 A in this ideal model.
nodes.mechanism: The final capstone must let you investigate and choose a repair path, not just recognise this example.
nodes.bridge: Return to the meter detective episode for extra probe positions if you want them.

debrief.title: A diagnosis earns its name
debrief.body: You used current and potential-difference evidence to separate two plausible faults, verified a repair against a predicted current, and made two fresh fault decisions. The final station repair still needs an open investigation workspace.

debrief.title: The station has two sound repairs
debrief.body: A pair of 24 ohm loads in parallel and a pair of 6 ohm loads in series can each draw 1 A from 12 V and transfer 6 W per load. Their socket voltages and currents differ. Explore both when you return, and use the fresh checks to test what carries across panels.

nodes.title: The panel is quiet
nodes.prompt: The 12 V supply feeds a 24 ohm navigation module in one branch. The sensor socket is empty in the other branch. Before touching the board, predict the source ammeter reading.

options.text: 0.5 A, because the complete navigation branch still conducts.
options.feedback: Yes. The 24 ohm branch still has 12 V across it, so I = V/R = 0.5 A.

options.text: 0 A, because any open branch stops the whole parallel board.
options.feedback: An open parallel branch does not break another complete branch.

options.text: 1 A, because the empty sensor branch also draws 0.5 A.
options.feedback: An empty socket is an open gap, so that branch draws no current.

hints: Trace only the navigation branch from one supply terminal to the other.
At fixed 12 V, use I = V/R for the intact 24 ohm branch.
nodes.workedExample: For a complete 24 ohm branch across 12 V, I = 12/24 = 0.5 A. The empty branch adds 0 A.
nodes.mechanism: A parallel open leaves the other closed branch available. In a series path, an open would stop both.
nodes.bridge: Review the parallel-routes and fault-board investigations if the two cases feel similar.

nodes.title: Wake the two rails
nodes.prompt: The practice board starts with one path and an empty sensor socket. Make the navigation load transfer about 12 W, give the sensor about 0.5 A, and bring source current to about 1.5 A. You may inspect readings before or after moving parts.
hints: In one path, an empty socket breaks the whole loop. Try connecting the sockets as branches.
A 12 ohm load across 12 V draws 1 A. A 24 ohm load across 12 V draws 0.5 A.
nodes.workedExample: Connect the sockets as branches. Leave the 12 ohm navigation load in place and put the 24 ohm sensor load in the open socket. The source then carries 1.5 A.
nodes.mechanism: The ideal 12 V supply holds both branches at 12 V. Their currents add at the source, while each load has its own power.
nodes.bridge: The series-path and parallel-routes episodes show the current and potential difference rules.

nodes.title: What changed?
nodes.prompt: The sensor wakes on its own branch. Why can the navigation current stay at 1 A while the source current rises to 1.5 A?

options.text: The ideal supply keeps 12 V across each branch. The sensor adds 0.5 A at the junction.
options.feedback: Exactly. The other branch does not steal current in this fixed-voltage model.

options.text: The branches share one fixed 1 A current, so each takes 0.5 A.
options.feedback: Separate complete branches share potential difference, not one fixed branch current.

options.text: The second branch creates new charge at the junction.
options.feedback: Charge is conserved. The source supplies the sum of the branch currents.

hints: Compare the navigation branch before and after adding the sensor.
Which quantity stays fixed across parallel branches in an ideal fixed-voltage supply?
nodes.workedExample: At 12 V, the 12 ohm branch draws 1 A. Adding a separate 24 ohm branch adds 0.5 A to the source, without changing that 1 A.
nodes.mechanism: A junction redirects charge flow; it does not create charge.
nodes.bridge: Revisit parallel-routes for branch potential difference and junction current.

nodes.title: Bring the station back online
nodes.prompt: Both service sockets need about 6 W each, and the 12 V source must draw about 1 A overall. The board starts with one 24 ohm module working and an empty socket. Choose components from the tray, change the wiring if useful, and inspect whatever readings help. More than one sound repair exists.
hints: Measure the source before moving anything, then ask what extra power the empty socket needs.
One route uses two 24 ohm modules on separate branches. Another uses two 6 ohm modules in one path. Check the potential difference across each socket.
nodes.workedExample: Route A: two 24 ohm loads in parallel each receive 12 V and transfer 6 W, drawing 0.5 A each. Route B: two 6 ohm loads in series share 12 V, each receiving 6 V at 1 A and transferring 6 W. Both make 12 W at the source.
nodes.mechanism: The same total power can come from different topology and resistance. The source current alone cannot tell you which repair was made.
nodes.bridge: Use meter-detective to plan a useful observation, then power-budget to connect watts with volts and amps.

nodes.title: A new storm clue
nodes.prompt: On a fresh 15 V panel, a 15 ohm main branch and a 30 ohm backup branch were both working. The backup suddenly opens. Which reading should the source ammeter now show?

options.text: 1 A. The main branch still draws 1 A, while the open backup draws 0 A.
options.feedback: Yes. The ideal source still holds 15 V across the intact main branch.

options.text: 1.5 A. The source current cannot change when a branch opens.
options.feedback: The missing backup had contributed 0.5 A before it opened.

options.text: 0 A. The broken backup stops every branch.
options.feedback: A parallel break only removes that branch when the main route remains closed.

hints: Calculate the current in each branch before the backup opens.
At 15 V, the intact 15 ohm branch draws 1 A. An open branch draws 0 A.
nodes.workedExample: Before the fault, 15/15 + 15/30 = 1.5 A. Afterwards, only 15/15 = 1 A remains.
nodes.mechanism: This is a new panel, so the earlier board settings cannot answer it for you.
nodes.bridge: Return to fault-board if a parallel open still looks like a complete break.

nodes.title: Close the logbook
nodes.prompt: A different 10 V source supplies 1 A for 6 s. Which pair correctly describes charge passing a point and energy transferred by the source?

options.text: 6 C and 60 J.
options.feedback: Yes. Q = It = 6 C, and E = VIt = 60 J.

options.text: 60 C and 6 J.
options.feedback: The units are reversed. Charge comes from current times time; energy also includes voltage.

options.text: 6 C and 6 J.
options.feedback: The charge is right, but each coulomb transfers 10 J at 10 V.

hints: Current counts coulombs per second. Potential difference counts joules per coulomb.
First find Q = I x t. Then use E = V x Q.
nodes.workedExample: At 1 A for 6 s, 6 C passes. Each coulomb transfers 10 J at 10 V, so the energy is 60 J.
nodes.mechanism: The two fresh checks are provisional evidence, not a certificate of whole-course mastery.
nodes.bridge: Review charge-counter and energy-lift for the unit meanings.
